claims.text: The modeled system is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The initial coating is perfectly crystalline and contains no pre-existing defects.
Nanoindentation is performed to 30 Å at 10 m/s and at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
Above 900 K, deformation changes from thermally activated dislocation annihilation to localized shear-induced amorphization at the contact interface.
High temperature suppresses the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu.
At high strain rate, the FeNiCrCoCu alloy cannot sustain a stable dislocation network.
Above 900 K, thermal energy exceeds the activation barriers for dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Activation of dislocation climb and cross-slip causes rapid dislocation annihilation and mechanical annealing.
Reduced stacking-fault energy promotes stacking faults and partial-dislocation activity.
Partial dislocations rapidly merge or annihilate, preventing work hardening.
Dislocation annihilation and stacking-fault collapse produce a localized loss of shear strength that triggers amorphization.
Adhesive bonding by the amorphous surface layer causes the friction-coefficient spike.
The amorphization process causes a catastrophic loss of wear resistance above 900 K.
The friction coefficient decreases between 300 K and 600 K because dislocation mobility increases.
The friction coefficient rises sharply at 900 K and 1200 K.
HCP-like atom counts transiently increase before the amorphous transition.
Dislocation line length in the contact zone falls to near zero at 1200 K.
At 600 K, dislocation density is reduced by thermal annealing while crystalline integrity is retained.
If stabilizing the stacking-fault energy eliminates the 900 K friction spike, then stacking-fault-energy reduction is not the primary driver.
If the friction spike persists at 1200 K after reducing indentation velocity to 0.1 m/s, the response is attributable to thermal softening rather than shear-induced amorphization.

contradictions.description: The mechanism identifies reduced stacking-fault energy as a primary cause of the friction spike, but the falsification rule says that eliminating the spike by preventing the reduction would disprove that cause. Elimination under the targeted intervention would instead support the claim that stacking-fault-energy reduction is necessary.
